nameStory: The 'spiderwort' name comes from the plant's long, thin leaves that arch gracefully like spider legs, and its old use as a remedy for spider bites (though we don't recommend that today!). The sticky, stringy sap that oozes from broken stems also resembles spider webs, adding to the arachnid connection.
description: Virginia spiderwort is a clump-forming perennial wildflower that grows 1-3 feet tall with grass-like leaves and showy three-petaled flowers. The bright blue, purple, or occasionally white flowers bloom at the tips of the stems in small clusters, each flower lasting only a day before closing. It's a native plant that spreads by underground rhizomes to form colonies, making it popular in wildflower gardens and naturalized areas.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Three rounded petals in bright blue, purple, pink, or white with prominent golden-yellow stamens in the center. Each flower is about 1 inch across and lasts only one day, opening in morning and closing by afternoon.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Long, narrow, grass-like leaves that fold lengthwise down the middle like a taco. They feel smooth and slightly succulent, growing 8-15 inches long and wrapping around the stem at the base.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms upright clumps 1-3 feet tall that gradually spread outward. The jointed stems have a bamboo-like appearance with swollen nodes where leaves attach.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thick, succulent stems that feel smooth and break easily with a distinctive 'snap.' When broken, they ooze a clear, stringy, mucilaginous sap that feels slippery between your fingers.

habitat: Virginia spiderwort thrives in rich, moist soils in partial shade to full sun, often found along woodland edges, meadows, and stream banks. It's commonly seen in gardens where it has escaped cultivation, and along roadsides and disturbed areas where the soil stays reasonably moist.

seasonality.spring: Fresh green shoots emerge early, with the distinctive folded leaves unfurling as temperatures warm. Flower buds begin forming in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming period from June through August, with clusters of three-petaled flowers opening fresh each morning. The plant is at its most recognizable during this time.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and small capsule fruits develop. Leaves begin yellowing and the plant starts dying back to its underground rhizomes.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground portions die back completely, leaving only dried stems. The plant survives underground and can be identified by location if you marked summer colonies.

funFact: Each spiderwort flower is nature's perfect day-timer - it opens with the morning sun and closes forever by mid-afternoon, never to reopen, which is why you'll often see fresh flowers and closed, wilted ones on the same plant!
confusionNotes: The grass-like leaves can make non-flowering plants look like ornamental grasses or even iris shoots, but spiderwort leaves fold in half lengthwise and have that distinctive succulent feel. The jointed, bamboo-like stems with swollen nodes are a dead giveaway.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Virginia' spiderwort, it's native throughout much of eastern North America, not just Virginia. The plant is also known as 'lady's tears' because of the clear, teardrop-like sap that weeps from broken stems.
compareHints: Virginia spiderwort is the most common spiderwort in New England and has the classic blue-purple flowers and smooth leaves. Ohio spiderwort, when present, tends to have hairier leaves and stems. The exotic purple heart has solid purple leaves and is only found as a houseplant or in containers.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Ohio spiderwort differs from Virginia spiderwort mainly in its hairless sepals and slightly more robust growth habit.

Compared to Virginia spiderwort (the most common spiderwort in New England), longbract spiderwort has much longer bracts extending well beyond the flower clusters, while Ohio spiderwort has hairless leaves (longbract's are slightly hairy).
Unlike its native New England spiderwort cousins like Virginia spiderwort, Purple Heart has distinctly purple foliage year-round rather than green leaves.
Unlike our native Virginia spiderwort with its grass-like leaves and blue flowers, inchplant has broad, striped leaves and rarely flowers indoors.
